claims.text: The stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior of HfNbTaTiZr is governed by internal residual stresses produced by thermal-expansion mismatch.
The relevant thermal-expansion mismatch occurs between a distorted solid-solution matrix and nanoscale compositional fluctuations or incipient precipitates.
HfNbTaTiZr contains compositional segregation or precipitate-related heterogeneity after solidification and cooling.
As-cast HfNbTaTiZr is a single-phase BCC alloy.
The as-cast BCC matrix has inherent lattice distortion.
Chemical inhomogeneities create nanoscale regions with different thermal-expansion coefficients.
Slow cooling or controlled annealing and cooling will accentuate thermal-expansion mismatch and increase internal residual stress.
Rapid quenching will minimize thermal-expansion mismatch and internal residual stress.
Differential thermal expansion between the matrix and nanoscale compositional or precipitate variations produces internal residual-stress fields.
Mismatch-induced internal stresses hinder dislocation motion through enhanced solute drag or pinning.
Mismatch-induced internal stresses modify the alloy's elastic moduli and thermoelastic response.
The proposed residual-stress mechanism unifies the reported creep, cold-rolling hardening, aging, and temperature-dependent elastic behavior.
Slow-cooled samples will have higher high-temperature yield strength than rapidly quenched samples.
Slow-cooled samples will have lower high-temperature creep rates than rapidly quenched samples.
Slow-cooled and quenched samples will exhibit measurably different elastic-modulus behavior between 293 and approximately 1100 K.
Slow-cooled samples may exhibit greater hardening during aging because of an interplay between precipitate stability and residual stress.
An unusual high-temperature strength plateau has been observed in the related NbTaTiZrV0.5 alloy.
The relative contributions of thermal-expansion mismatch, oxidation, and precipitation-induced hardening are not quantitatively known.
